lines.text: Chapter four, section five. Scenario, bet-check-bet.
So far we have talked about betting the turn after betting the flop, but what happens when you bet the flop, check the turn, and then get to face a river decision?
This is the bet-check line, and it is much more common than novices expect, especially on turns that are bad for the c-bettor's range.
By checking the turn, you preserve the option to fold cheaply, and you also let some of your medium-strength hands realize their equity for free.

Importantly, you keep leverage alive for the river: after your check, your opponent's range still has to worry about your polarized river betting range, particularly on turns where you would clearly value bet with the top of your range.
When the river card arrives, ask two questions.
First, does this river card change the balance of the ranges enough to justify a big polarized bet from you?
Second, if your opponent bets into you, is her betting range a real polarized range, or is it a thin value plus rare bluff shape that you should mostly call against?

The bet-check-bet line combines pot control on the turn with a targeted river attack, and it is one of the most valuable sequences to master, because it lets a hand like top pair mediocre kicker still profit even on tough turns.
The rule of thumb is: check the turn when the card damages your range's balance, and choose your river bet size based on how much of your range remains truly polarized after the runout.
